findings.title: New isinstance guard can silently skip killing unhealthy multiprocessing flusher processes
findings.body: In `_ensure_processes_alive()` the new code guards `process.kill()` with `if isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process):`. The processes are actually created via `self.mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, so they are instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. On platforms/configurations where the *default* multiprocessing context is not spawn (e.g. fork on Linux, which is Sentry's typical deployment target), `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to a different class (e.g. `ForkProcess`), and `isinstance(spawn_process, multiprocessing.Process)` evaluates to False. Previously (pre-PR) `kill()` was called unconditionally, so this guard is new and can silently prevent an unhealthy/hung child process from ever being killed before a replacement process is spawned for the same shards. The result is two processes concurrently flushing/producing the same shard's segments, risking duplicate production to the buffered-segments topic (data integrity) and leaked/zombie OS processes.

findings.title: join() aborts terminating remaining flusher processes once a deadline is hit mid-loop
findings.body: In `join(timeout)`, the loop over `self.processes.items()` breaks out entirely as soon as the deadline is exceeded for the process currently being iterated (`if remaining_time <= 0: break`). This skips the `process.terminate()` call for all subsequent process indexes in the dict, not just the one that timed out. With a single flusher process (pre-PR behavior) this was not an issue, but with multiple flusher processes per shard group, hitting the timeout while waiting on an early process means later processes are never explicitly terminated during this shutdown path (e.g. during a strategy teardown/rebalance where the whole interpreter does not exit), leaving them running as orphaned subprocesses.

findings.title: Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op due to earlier global monkeypatch, so it doesn't actually fix the intended race
findings.body: The test patches `time.sleep` globally at line 15 (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), which replaces the `sleep` attribute on the actual `time` module for the duration of the test. The newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` at line 62, intended to "give flusher threads time to process after drift change," therefore does nothing — it resolves to the same monkeypatched no-op. The test's reliability against the race between updating `current_drift` and the background flusher thread observing it relies solely on incidental GIL/thread scheduling from the extra `step.poll()` call, not on any real wait, so the fix may not reliably prevent flakiness it was meant to address.

findings.title: Inconsistent metric tag key between related timers ("shard" vs "shards")
findings.body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` metrics use tag key `"shard"` (lines 185, 195), while the `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer at line 199 uses tag key `"shards"` (plural). This inconsistency means dashboards/alerts built around one tag name won't match the other metric, making it harder to correlate produce time with wait-for-produce time per shard.

findings.title: Docstring overstates that one process is created per shard
findings.body: The class docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing," but the implementation actually creates `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))` processes and distributes shards round-robin across them via `process_to_shards_map`, so multiple shards commonly share a single process (as also demonstrated by `test_flusher_processes_limit`). The docstring should clarify that shards are distributed across up to `max_processes` processes, not necessarily one process per shard.
